content.title: Common response to all the reviewers
content.comment:
We appreciate all the reviewers for their valuable comments. We believe our manuscript will become clearer and stronger by incorporating your comments, although we have decided to withdraw the current submission for now. In this letter, nevertheless, we clarify some of the major comments raised from the reviewers.

**[8gS6, dHs6] Comparison with DisenIB (Pan et al., 2021)?**

DisenIB does not address our key motivation of making $\mathbf{z}$ to learn every $\mathbf{y}$-correlated signal in $\mathbf{x}$. For your information, we also provide a direct comparison with DisenIB in Appendix H to confirm this. Specifically, DisenIB aims to optimize the following:

$$\max I(\mathbf{z};\mathbf{y}) + I(\mathbf{x}; \mathbf{z}_n, \mathbf{y}) - I(\mathbf{z}_n; \mathbf{z}).$$ 

Here, a key difference compared to our proposed NIB (Eq. 4) is in their reconstruction terms: i.e., $I(\mathbf{x}; \mathbf{z}\_n, \mathbf{y})$ of DisenIB vs. $I(\mathbf{x}; \mathbf{z}, \mathbf{z}\_n)$ of NIB. Due to this difference, DisenIB cannot rule out the cases when $\mathbf{z}$ only encode few of shortcut signals in $\mathbf{x}$ (correlated to $\mathbf{y}$) even at its optimum.

**[8gS6] Evaluation is limited to corruption-type shifts?**

We note that our ImageNet experiments given in Table 5 not only reports the corruption-like ImageNet-C, but also covers ImageNet-R (rendition) and ImageNet-Sketch, both of which consider samples that are semantically far from those of the original ImageNet. As you mentioned, our noisy channel model in Eq. (3) indeed suggests a quite general framework on distribution shifts, and we believe it is an important future work to develop a better approximation of the threat model to address a wider notion of distribution shifts more effectively.

**[8gS6] MNIST -> SVHN: What AENIB considers as OOD?**

Remark that AENIB utilize both $\mathbf{z}$ and $\mathbf{z}\_n$ to define its OOD score for novelty detection (Section 3.1). Although $\mathbf{z}$ in AENIB is trained to be robust against distribution shifts, there is no such restriction for $\mathbf{z}\_n$: i.e., the score from $\mathbf{z}\_n$ can still be sensitive against the shifts. Ideally, one should design an OOD score that is calibrated with respect to the semantic distance: in fact, the OBJECT benchmark reported in Table 1 evaluates such scenarios, by incorporating near-in-distribution datasets into the standard benchmark.

**[dPLo] Unclear motivation**

Although we agree with your point on why the problem of shaping an “optimal” nuisance is extremely challenging, we think this does not imply our motivation is “contradictory”. Essentially, learning more signals in a representation does not automatically imply an over-fitting. Rather, it implies that the relative importance of each signal will be decreased, and so it should be regarded as an “ensemble” of the signals (e.g., similarly to how Dropout improves generalization). The capacity constraint of information bottleneck is still essential to our framework (even though we aim to keep more information as mentioned by Reviewer dPLo), as we still require the representation to be simple enough to perform classification, e.g., with a linear classifier.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper claims that the standard information bottleneck framework can fail in out-of-distribution scenarios as it can essentially learn one signal that is correlated with $y$ in training, while ignoring all others. Authors extend this framework for learning more robust representations by introducing a nuisance representation $z_n$ along with the standard input representation $z$. Essentially, the nuisance factor is trained to capture all the “remaining” information about the input $x$, not correlated with label y. Authors propose practical loss functions and novel architectures for nuisance modeling and perform extensive quantitative evaluation in a variety of tasks.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:

1. Considering the information bottleneck framework under distribution-shift scenarios is interesting and novel. I like the insight that the penalty in IB to minimize $I(z; x)$ can essentially learn a model that hones in on a single shortcut signal instead of all correlated signals. 
2. Empirical evaluation is provided on a variety of tasks: OOD detection, natural corruption robustness and adversarial robustness.

Weaknesses:

1. My main concern is regarding the out-of-distribution framework using the noisy channel model in Equation (3). 
   1. It is a very general framework that allows for much harder shifts as long as the semantic information is maintained, i.e., $I(x; y) = I(\hat{x}; y)$. For example, standard MNIST to colored MNIST (say, all digits are colored red), or MNIST digits to SVHN style digits are allowed in the framework. However, I do not think the proposed method is capable of such OOD robustness. 
   2. While the paper claims OOD robustness without any prior assumption/model for the OOD shift, it seems from experiments that the proposed method has some implicit assumptions that helps for corruption-type OOD shifts (e.g., different types of noises but relatively close to the original image in L2 distance) but not other types of OOD shifts. 
   3. A related problem with OOD detection experiments is what the model considers to be OOD. For instance, all corruptions (natural/adversarial), MNIST->SVHN, etc. are technically OOD. Can the model **detect** these shifts, while also being **robust** to them? Seems like they are competing objectives and it is unclear how the model does both. 
2. Empirical evaluation can be improved with stronger baselines (details below). 



**Other questions**

1. While I can intuitively see why the standard IB model will learn only one of the many shortcut signals, the paper can be strengthened with a simple experiment that clearly showcases this. In the current experiments, it is unclear if this is the reason for the failure of VIB. 

2. Equations (5-7) are used to satisfy the conditions for Lemma 1, which then guarantees that $I(z; y) = I(x; y)$. Then, does one need the full $R_\text{IB}$ objective that maximizes $I(z; y)$ again?

3. Experimental evaluation with other baselines: Since there are several works that model nuisance factors (as discussed by the authors in the related work like Jaiswal et al., 2018; 2019; Pan et al., 2021), these should be added as baselines for the experiments in the main paper (in Tables 1-5). 

4. From the experiment section, I am unable to ascertain whether the performance improvement is due to the proposed architecture (FSD) or due to the nuisance modeling framework. The ablation study in Appendix D does not address this. 

5. OOD detection experiments: VIB performs better than AENIB as long as we compare using the same scores. Is it possible for VIB to use $\mathcal{N}(z; 0, I)$ score additionally (similar to $\mathcal{N}(z_n; 0, I)$ for AENIB)?

6. Minor: The choice of using Equation (6) to force the distribution toward “uniform” instead of the standard adversarial formulation should be discussed/justified in the paper. Similarly, the choice of Equation (7) to induce independence instead of other methods (e.g., directly minimizing mutual information) should be discussed.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is very well written and sufficient information is provided for reproducibility.
content.summary_of_the_review: The out-of-distribution framework using the noisy channel model in Equation (3) allows for much harder shifts but the proposed method is not capable of solving (i.e., not shown theoretically/empirically). I tend to disagree with the claim of OOD robustness without prior model for the type of OOD shift as there seems to be implicit assumptions that help the model in corruption-type OOD shifts. While the empirical evaluation was performed on a variety of tasks, stronger set of baselines, like existing nuisance-based IB frameworks, should be considered.

content.summary_of_the_paper: In machine learning, the Information Bottleneck (IB) principle is often used to train deep neural networks and learn efficient representations. Efficiency in this context refers to a latent representation $z$ that is maximally informative about some target variable $y$ while being maximally compressive about the input variable $x$. In practice this idea is enabled by maximizing the so called IB-objective: $I(z,y)$ – $\beta\times I(z,x)$, where $I(\cdot)$ denotes the mutual information, and $\beta\geq0$ is a hyperparameter controlling the capacity of $z$. In this paper, the authors argue that in practice, due to the presence of possibly predictive biases in the data, the original IB formulation can result in representations $z$ encoding predictive-yet-compressible information (referred to as shortcut signals in the paper), which would hinder robustness and generalization to out-of-distribution (OOD) examples. To mitigate this issue, the authors introduce a nuisance latent variable $z_n$  complementing $z$  in reconstructing the input $x$  while being encouraged to be minimally expressive about the target variable $y$ .  The main objective of the proposed approach is to encourage the latent variable $z$  to encode any information from $x$  that is correlated with $y$  and not only shortcut signals. The proposed method referred to as nuisance extended IB (NIB) is used to train autoencoder architectures, which are evaluated on several image datasets in terms of OOD detection, robustness against natural and adversarial corruptions.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths. 
- The paper is well written and technically sound. 
- This work tries to mitigate a significant limitation of the IB method in the context of deep learning, namely a bias towards encoding only spurious correlations between $x$ and $y$ in the latent variable $z$. 
- Compared to the chosen baselines on the tasks of OOD detection and robustness against data corruptions, Autoencoder architectures trained using the NIB objective offer competitive performance in several cases. 

Weaknesses.       
- The novelty of this work is somewhat limited. The idea described in this paper to improve the robustness of the IB method is very close to that of Disentangled IB [1].  
- Some aspects of the proposed method deserve more clarification and justification. For, instance why is the independence between $z_n$ and $z$ enforced a priori and not a posteriori (given $x$). To improve robustness of the IB method, is the introduction of the nuisance variable $z_n$ necessary? That is, how about dropping $z_n$ in eq. 4? I would recommend completing the ablation study of Appendix D by the latter scenario. 
- The dependency structure between the different random variables is not explicitly stated. I would recommend improving this aspect, for instance by including the corresponding graphical model. 

[1] Pan, Ziqi, et al. "Disentangled information bottleneck." Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence. Vol. 35. No. 10. 2021.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes a reformulation of an information bottleneck objective for improving robustness of the learned representation under various changes (distribution shifts, natural and adversarial corruptions). The core idea is to add components to the standard information bottleneck objective, that are encouraging the learned representation to consist of two parts: main and nuisance, such that input can be reconstructed from such representation, the parts of representation are independent and the predictive ability of nuisance part is minimal. The proposed loss is used for convolutional variational encoders and also can be used for transformers based architectures. It is evaluated on the task of OOD against simple crossentropy and standard variational information bottleneck objective; on the task of corruption robustness and on the task of adversarial robustness.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The paper addresses an interesting problem of encouraging more robustness through information bottleneck loss.

One of the large problems of the paper is a very confusing motivation for all the proposed architecture choices and loss enhancements. The details are given below in the "Clarity" part.
The provided theoretical result seems to be proven under a not possible condition. I see a lot of problems with Lemma1. First of all, there introduced an additional condition, that was not mentioned anywhere before in the description of the method, about independence of main part of representation and nuisance part. Second, there is no reference to the proof in the appendix. Third, and most critical, the proof assumes f being inverse, that is not true for the stochastic neural networks and if it would have been true, then I(x,z) used in the optimization will become infinite.
Provided empirical evaluation benchmarks against standard loss and VIB, but not some SOTA for OOD or properly adversarially trained models.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The writing of the paper suffers from very long sentences with large amounts of i.e. and e.g. - especially the introduction and explanation of the approach.
Overall, it is very hard to follow the motivation for the proposed approach and multiple questions are raising:
1) The main idea of the information bottleneck is to get rid of the not needed information in the input data. Thus, the idea to reformulate information bottleneck loss in order to keep more information is confusing and seems contradictory. The main justification given is that there can be some duplicated information that is also predictive of a target, but not necessary for the training dataset at hand, while being necessary for some data with distribution shift. While it can be the case, the continuation is that there is also nuisance in the input that is not needed for the task. I do not understand why in some cases of distribution shifts nuisances in the initial task cannot become important if some duplicated information can. Another, parallel motivation provided in the paper is the overfitting of the information bottleneck method to "shortcut" signals. This motivation is even more contradictory, because then learning all the signals leading to label in the dataset at hand is even more overfitting than before.
2) The motivation for including reconstruction error is not clearly justified as well.
3) The explanation of the architecture building using convolutional statistics is very confusing in the introduction, as well as transformer based paths.
4) Why the proposed representations can learn "more semantic information" as it is claimed in the introduction (last paragraph)?
5) The phrase that the proposed method gives an adversarial protection "for free by applying randomized smoothing" is extremely confusing, since randomized smoothing is a type of adversarial protection, then what exactly is got for free?
6) There seems to be a typo in the explanation of the equation (2) - it is the description of encoder, not decoder.
7) There seems to be a typo in the description of equation (3) - it is minimization problem, not minimax.
8) It is unclear to me, why minimization of the mutual information of label with nuisance parts of the representation is "adversarial behavior". While it is clear that minimizing information between label and representation while keeping mutual information between label and input is kind of a poisoning, nuisance is told to be not predictive about label at all - so it anyway has no information about label.
9) There seems to be a formulation problem in the sentence describing Lemma1.
10) Section 2.1 introduces the computable version of the loss proposed, but the explanations in all three parts are not enough for understanding how the proposed values approximate mutual information of interest.
11) The experiments section on checking the OOD detection introduces multiple additional tricks to the method, which are not explained or described in details before. The best results for corruption robustness are also achieved using the proposed method and additional methods on top.
12) Motivation for using certificate robustness as verification that the proposed method is adversarially robust is unclear: "it is hard to get non-trivial accuracy without a thorough adversarial training". It is clear that the model has to be somehow robust to get non-trivial accuracy when being attacked and certification should in general reflect this property. Thus claiming that certification is more suitable for checking robustness is incorrect.

The idea of adding nuisance learning in the information bottleneck objective is novel.

The code is not provided, but all the details of the experiments are given. Taking into account the complexity of the approach the reproducibility might be hard.
content.summary_of_the_review: The proposed enhancement of the variational information bottleneck for encouraging robustness is very weakly motivated and not followed by substantial theoretical justification. The provided empirical evaluation demonstrates benefits of the proposed method combined with additional engineering enhancements, not mentioned in the description of the method. The method is evaluated against standard crossentropy and VIB, but not specific SOTA in the areas.

content.title: Learning Robust Representations via Nuisance-extended Information Bottleneck
content.abstract: The information bottleneck (IB) is a principled approach to obtain a succinct representation $\mathbf{x} \rightarrow \mathbf{z}$ for a given downstream task $\mathbf{x} \rightarrow \mathbf{y}$: namely, it finds $\mathbf{z}$ that (a) maximizes the (task-relevant) mutual information $I(\mathbf{z}; \mathbf{y})$, while (b) minimizing $I(\mathbf{x}; \mathbf{z})$ to constrain the capacity of $\mathbf{z}$ for better generalization. In practical scenarios where the training data is limited, however, many predictive-yet-compressible signals in the data can be rather from some biases in data acquisition (i.e., less generalizable), so that even the IB objective cannot prevent $\mathbf{z}$ from co-adapting on such (so-called) "shortcut" signals. To bypass such a failure mode, we consider an adversarial threat model of $\mathbf{x}$ under constraint on the mutual information $I(\mathbf{x}; \mathbf{y})$. This motivates us to extend IB to additionally model the nuisance information against $\mathbf{z}$, namely $\mathbf{z}_n$, so that $(\mathbf{z}, \mathbf{z}_n)$ can reconstruct $\mathbf{x}$. To enable the idea, we propose an auto-encoder based training upon the variational IB framework, as well as practical encoder designs to facilitate the proposed hybrid discriminative-generative training considering both convolutional- and Transformer-based architectures. Our experimental results show that the proposed scheme improves robustness of learned representations (remarkably without using any domain-specific knowledge), with respect to multiple challenging modern security measures including novelty detection, corruption (or natural) robustness and certified adversarial robustness.
